migrationNotes: Spine: a bike braking from two speeds. The brakes remove everything the bike has because it moves, which gives kinetic energy and the formula ½mv², then the squared speed explains stopping distances, and net work becomes the change in kinetic energy.

lesson.title: Energy of motion

lead.text: Brakes press on the wheel and produce a force against the bike's motion. That force acts over the stopping distance, so it does negative work on the bike: the braking force times the distance, with a minus sign. By the time the bike has stopped, the brakes have removed everything it had because it was moving.

That quantity needs a name. It is called kinetic energy, the amount an object holds because of its motion. We can measure it by asking how much work it takes to bring the object to rest, and it is counted in joules, like work. A bike at rest has none, and a faster bike has more.

With a steady braking force, the kinetic energy equals the braking force times the stopping distance. For the same brakes, a bike with more kinetic energy has to travel further before it stops. What remains is to find how the kinetic energy depends on the bike's mass and speed.

Take a 3 kg cart rolling at 2 m/s and brake it with a steady 3 N. The second law gives an acceleration of 3 ÷ 3 = 1 m/s² against the motion, so the cart stops after 2 s. Its speed falls steadily from 2 m/s to 0, which makes its average speed 1 m/s, so it travels 1 × 2 = 2 m. The brakes do 3 × 2 = 6 J of work. The cart began with 6 J of kinetic energy.

Doing the same sum with letters gives the general rule. A mass m at speed v is braked by a steady force F. Its acceleration is a = F ÷ m, it stops in a time v ÷ a, and it covers the average speed, v ÷ 2, times that time. The work F times that distance simplifies, using F = ma, to half the mass times the speed squared.

afterFigure.text: Check the cart against the formula: ½ × 3 × 2² = 6 J. The speed is squared and the mass is not, and that difference decides almost everything that follows. Kinetic energy is never negative, and it does not depend on which way the object moves.

lead.text: For the same brakes, the stopping distance is the kinetic energy divided by the braking force.

reveal.text: Twice the speed means four times the kinetic energy to remove, so the stopping distance is four times as long.

lead.text: A 2 kg cart moves at 3 m/s. Use the formula from the last screen.

reveal.text: You squared the speed, multiplied by the mass and halved it: ½ × 2 × 9 gives 9 J.

steps.headline: Why speed counts for more than mass

lead.text: The squared speed has consequences you can feel on the road. A car at 60 km/h has four times the kinetic energy of the same car at 30 km/h. Its brakes have to remove four times as much, and with the same braking force it needs four times the distance. A modest drop in speed shortens the stopping distance by a lot, which is why speed limits near schools are low.

Mass enters the formula once, so it has a gentler effect. A loaded lorry and an empty one at the same speed differ in kinetic energy in proportion to their masses, and the loaded one needs more from its brakes. Both matter, but doubling the speed does far more than doubling the mass.
Braking is one case of a general rule. The net work done on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy, the final value minus the initial value.

A 5 kg trolley speeds up from 2 m/s to 4 m/s. Its kinetic energy rises from ½ × 5 × 2² = 10 J to ½ × 5 × 4² = 40 J, so the net work done on it is 40 − 10 = +30 J. Let it slow from 4 m/s back to 2 m/s and the net work is −30 J. Positive net work speeds an object up and negative net work slows it down. A bike that brakes to rest loses all its kinetic energy, so the net work on it is minus its starting kinetic energy.
A 2 kg cart is pushed until it goes faster. Find the energy at each speed first.

reveal.text: Net work is the gain in kinetic energy, from 9 J to 25 J.

lead.text: Keep the speed fixed and change the mass instead.

reveal.text: Mass enters ½mv² once, so energy scales with mass directly. Speed is the term that is squared.

lesson.orientation: Use kinetic energy and net work to connect force with a change in speed.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Ride a bike slowly, at about 3 m/s, squeeze the brakes hard and it stops in about a metre. Now ride at twice that speed and squeeze just as hard. The bike does not stop in twice the distance. It runs on much further than that, which is why a fast car needs so much more room than a slow one.

The last lesson gave us a way to count what a force does as it acts over a distance. Brakes are a force acting over a distance, and they finish with the bike at rest. So the work the brakes do must be tied to how fast the bike was going, and that link should explain the surprise.

We start from the brakes and find what a moving object has that they remove. Then we write it as a formula, use the formula to follow the bike at two speeds, and say what the net work on any object changes about its motion.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find an object's kinetic energy and say how net work changes it.

recap.keyIdea: Kinetic energy is ½mv², so it grows with the square of the speed. Net work equals the change in kinetic energy.

blocks.text: You found that a bike at twice the speed needs four times the stopping distance and that a 2 kg cart at 3 m/s has 9 J. Speeding that cart up from 3 m/s to 5 m/s took 16 J of net work.

recap.nextHook: A bike freewheeling down a hill speeds up with nobody pedalling, so something other than movement must be supplying its kinetic energy. Next we find how much a height difference stores.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart moves at 3 m/s. Find its kinetic energy in joules.
hints: Kinetic energy uses speed squared.
Use K = ½mv².
Square the speed, multiply by mass, then take half.
questions.onCorrect: 9 J. Square the speed first, then multiply by the mass and take half.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the half. Kinetic energy is ½mv².
That squares the product of mass and speed instead of the speed alone.
That is the speed. Kinetic energy is ½mv².

questions.prompt: A cart's speed doubles while its mass stays fixed. By what factor does its kinetic energy increase?
hints: Mass is fixed, so only the speed term changes.
Doubling the speed doubles v before it is squared.
Square the 2.
questions.onCorrect: 4. The speed is squared, so doubling it multiplies kinetic energy by four.

misconceptions.feedback: That scales energy with speed. Kinetic energy depends on speed squared.
That would be speed cubed. Energy goes as speed squared.

questions.prompt: A cart's mass doubles while its speed stays fixed. What happens to its kinetic energy?
hints: Separate the first power of mass from the square of speed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mass enters K = ½mv² as a direct multiplier, so energy doubles.

questions.onCorrect: It doubles. Mass multiplies directly in ½mv², so twice the mass is twice the energy.

misconceptions.feedback: More mass at the same speed means more energy, not less.
Squaring applies to the speed, not the mass. Doubling the mass doubles the energy.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart speeds up from 3 m/s to 5 m/s. Find the net work done on it in joules.
hints: Calculate the final and initial kinetic energies.
Net work equals their difference.
Calculate 25 − 9.
questions.onCorrect: 16 J. Net work equals the change in kinetic energy: final minus initial.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the final kinetic energy alone. Net work is the change: final minus initial.
That uses the change in speed. Work is the change in ½mv².

questions.prompt: A 4 kg object moves at speed 5 m/s. Find its kinetic energy in joules.
hints: Square speed before multiplying.
Use the one-half factor.
Calculate 0.5 × 4 × 25.
questions.onCorrect: 50 J. Square the speed, multiply by the mass, take half.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the half. Kinetic energy is ½mv².
That uses the speed without squaring it.

questions.prompt: A cart initially has 50 J of kinetic energy and comes to rest. What net work is done on it?
hints: Use the energy change, including its sign.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Net work is final minus initial kinetic energy: 0 − 50 = −50 J.

questions.onCorrect: A loss of fifty joules. Net work is final minus initial kinetic energy: 0 − 50.

misconceptions.feedback: The cart lost energy, so the net work is negative, not a gain.
Its kinetic energy changed, so the net work is not zero. Net work equals that change.

questions.prompt: A bike's brakes stop it from 3 m/s in 1 m. The same brakes, with the same braking force, stop it from 6 m/s in how many metres?
hints: Does twice the speed mean twice the distance?
Think about how the energy to be removed grows with speed.
Squaring the speed makes the energy, and the distance, grow faster than the speed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Twice the speed means four times the energy to remove, so 4 m.

questions.onCorrect: 4 m. Twice the speed needs four times the stopping distance. The reason is kinetic energy, which depends on speed squared.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles the distance with the speed. The energy to remove grows faster than that.

questions.prompt: A 1 kg ball moves at 6 m/s. What is its kinetic energy in joules?
hints: Square the speed first.
Multiply by the mass.
Take half of the result.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the half.

questions.prompt: A cart's kinetic energy rises from 10 J to 25 J. What net work was done on it, in joules?
hints: Net work is the change in kinetic energy.
Final minus initial.
Take the first value from the second.
questions.onCorrect: 15 J. Net work equals the change in kinetic energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two energies. Net work is the change: final minus initial.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart slows from 5 m/s to 1 m/s. What net work is done on it, in joules?
hints: Find the kinetic energy before and after.
Net work is final minus initial.
The cart loses energy, so the answer is negative.
questions.onCorrect: −24 J. The cart loses kinetic energy, so the net work is negative.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the cart slowed. The net work is negative.
That uses the change in speed. Work is the change in ½mv².
